acceptance.status_reason: NOT SCORED PASS, AND THE GAP IS A DELIBERATE CONFLICT BETWEEN THIS CRITERION AND THE TO's OWN STANDING RULES. The only senders this work CHANGED are the password-reset and welcome mailers; the OTP mailer already used noreply@. Firing one therefore means either (a) sending unsolicited auth mail to a real person's mailbox, or (b) a test account on a live human address -- which standing rule 1 in this same TO forbids, because that is exactly what caused tonight's false bug report. Standing rule 2 separately forbids aiming an outbound-side-effect route at a live sender. A synthetic .invalid recipient sends but cannot be READ, so it cannot satisfy 'observed'. I am recording the conflict rather than resolving it by quietly breaking one of the two rules. The cheapest sound resolution is Andrew's word to fire one password reset at his own mailbox -- the same shape that closed W1-10 -- and it is put to him rather than assumed.

acceptance.criterion_verbatim: getUserPKByEmail with two records sharing one email returns a surfaced ambiguity rather than an arbitrary pick. Construct the collision -- a fixture with two rows, not an argument that it could happen. Then show the single-match path still returns normally (positive control).
acceptance.invocation: Wrote TWO PROFILE items sharing the email d12-w2-collision@opal.invalid into the live opal-users-v2, confirmed the email-index GSI returned 2, then POSTed /auth/login against the deployed handler. Deleted one row and repeated the IDENTICAL request.
acceptance.output_evidence: COLLISION CONSTRUCTED, not argued: GSI length(Items) = 2. TARGET (2 rows): HTTP 500, and the handler log names the path -- {"event":"user_lookup_ambiguous","pks":["USER#usr_w2collide02","USER#usr_w2collide01"],"count":2} followed by 'Account lookup is ambiguous'. POSITIVE CONTROL (1 row, byte-identical request): HTTP 401 {"error":"Invalid email or password"} with log {"event":"login_failed","reason":"bad_password"} -- the normal path, unchanged. Fixture fully removed afterwards: 48 PROFILE items, 0 collision rows remaining.
acceptance.denominator: 2 identical login requests; the ONLY variable is the number of rows sharing the email. 2 fixture rows created, 2 deleted.
acceptance.status_reason: The log line is what makes this sound rather than suggestive: a bare 500 is consistent with any handler error, so it would not by itself distinguish the ambiguity path from an unrelated failure. The named event with both PKs is the discriminator, and the 401 control shows the change did not simply break login for everyone. A synthetic .invalid address was used deliberately -- standing rule 1 forbids a live human address, and the ambiguity throws before any SES call so nothing was sent.

mutant.description: W2-3 IS ITSELF THE PLANTED MUTANT, which is why it is the strongest row here. The defect under test -- a duplicate email resolving nondeterministically -- does not occur naturally in the live table (48 emails, 48 distinct). Rather than argue it could happen, the duplicate state was CONSTRUCTED on the live table and the deployed handler was driven against it.
mutant.expected: With 2 rows sharing an email the handler surfaces the ambiguity by name and refuses; with 1 row the identical request behaves normally.
mutant.observed: 2 rows -> HTTP 500 with {"event":"user_lookup_ambiguous","pks":[both],"count":2}. 1 row -> HTTP 401 'Invalid email or password' with a normal login_failed log. Fixture removed; 0 collision rows remain.

determinism.method: The W2-3 pair is two byte-identical POSTs differing only in the row count behind the email. The running-bytes census was also taken after the apply and compared against the sha the build emitted.
determinism.observed: The ambiguity path fired on BOTH requests made while two rows existed (two separate request ids, 01:49:09.515Z and 01:49:09.780Z, same event, same PKs) and did not fire once one row was removed. Deployed sha matched the built sha exactly.
